title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation

paper.title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation
paper.abstract:
Abstract We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions , defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done rather than what should have been done, and where data is sparse, a model’s predictions may be too uncertain to act on.
In this work, we provide a framework for addressing this problem using a case study in deceased-donor kidney allocation.
Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. One can use AI to flag kidneys at risk of delayed or failed placement for out-of-sequence (OOS) allocation, but this comes at the cost of bypassing candidates higher on the waitlist. Thus, OOS allocation should only be used when the organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence.
Using Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network match-run data from 2016–2019 and 2023–2025 (excluding COVID-19-disrupted years), we build the Arbitrator framework, which combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. Our Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data, and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. We show that the Arbitrator correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as OOS candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement and potentially transplanted. We then exploit the interpretability of the Arbitrator to create an agentic audit comparing the learned rules to published clinical literature in order to flag decision-making patterns that are contentious. We discuss various future directions that stem from this advancement due to AI.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In 2023, nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States were not transplanted despite a persistent and overwhelming shortage of organs for patients with kidney failure [ 21 ] . The problem is not simply that all non-transplanted kidneys are medically unsuitable; rather, many of these organs are likely transplantable upon recovery [ 2 ] , but deteriorate over the length of time required for an organ procurement organization (OPO) to find a suitable match for the organ [ 7 ; 45 ; 3 ] . Under OPTN policy, a deceased donor kidney in the United States is offered sequentially to compatible candidates in a priority sequence, or match run , determined by national allocation rules [ 11 ] . This sequence is designed to make the organ offer process systematic, fair, and auditable. However, if OPOs believe that sequential offering is unlikely to succeed by the time the organ expires, they may choose to expedite placement via out-of-sequence (OOS) placement [ 17 ; 12 ] . This creates a tradeoff: adhering to the match run risks nonuse of hard-to-place organs, while OOS placement bypasses candidates with higher priority, undermining the fairness the match run is designed to ensure. The concern that OOS allocation processes may be unfair is not unmerited: recent work has documented socioeconomic differences among recipients of OOS kidneys [ 17 ; 18 ; 29 ] , and more work is needed to ensure OOS allocation is not exacerbating inequities in the healthcare system. A useful decision aid must therefore distinguish organs for which OOS allocation prevents nonuse from those easily matchable organs for which the standard sequence should be preserved. Machine learning (ML) and, more broadly, artificial intelligence (AI) are attractive tools for this problem because donor profiles are high dimensional and organ acceptance reflects nonlinear interactions between clinical characteristics. Predictive models have already been developed for kidney discard, delayed placement, and offer acceptance [ 27 ; 48 ; 4 ; 5 ; 43 ] . But the barrier to responsible deployment is not predictive performance alone. In a qualitative study of 23 healthcare professionals considering AI-driven clinical decision support for resource allocation, Yüksel Elgin and Elgin found recurring concerns about the cost of increased efficiency in terms of equity, transparency and explainability. Participants also stressed the need for additional review and manual oversight of AI decisions and emphasized that AI should be used for decision support rather than a replacement for clinical expertise [ 47 ] . It is evident that in high-stakes decisions, a model with high predictive accuracy on past data does not imply that the model’s learned behaviors are always worth replicating. AI models trained on historical outcomes can learn and reproduce the bias of the dataset when used for future high-stakes decisions [ 31 ] , and historical organ allocation decisions themselves show socioeconomic disparities [ 17 ; 29 ] . Beyond bias, decision guidelines can also become outdated with new research and evolving transplantation policy, meaning that a good decision using the best available information ten years ago may differ from a good decision using the best available information today. These concerns motivate a shift from prioritizing accuracy in prediction to generating uncertainty-aware prescription. That is, AI models must support decisions about not just how to intervene, but also whether to intervene based on the model’s limitations. Our work seeks to incorporate three relevant components when using AI to recommend kidneys for out-of-sequence allocation: interpretability, uncertainty-awareness, and validation from external evidence. We call this outcome early-matchability (EM), and we recommend that OOS allocation be considered when an organ is not likely to be EM. Given a relative preference β \beta for maintaining the match run versus routing high-risk organs OOS, the optimal action is to send an organ OOS if its EM probability is at most τ β \tau_{\beta} . However, a given ML/AI prediction is not guaranteed to be accurate, and different predictions can come with different levels of certainty based on the organ’s features. Our models are uncertainty-aware , which means that the model abstains from making a decision if its confidence interval for the EM probability contains τ β \tau_{\beta} ; that is, if the uncertainty in the estimated EM probability could change the recommended action. Otherwise, the model certifies either the on-sequence (OS) action (the full confidence interval lies above τ β \tau_{\beta} ) or the OOS action (the full confidence interval lies below τ β \tau_{\beta} ). Because we have multiple interpretable ML models, we use the Arbitrator decision rule to resolve their recommendations, submitting either a certified action or deferring the organs for additional review, which, in practice, can be done by humans. In this work, we defer the decision to a more powerful, but “black-box” XGBoost model. Finally, because each model outputs a set of interpretable decision rules, we audit each resolved recommendation for alignment with published medical literature instead of blindly replicating historical decisions. This helps us identify problematic trends learned by AI models from historic data. Our agentic auditor can make one of three decisions: (1) provisionally retain the proposed optimal action (decide), (2) propose considering the opposite action due to medical research (deviate), or (3) request additional review for the model rule and recommendation due to insufficient evidence (defer). This model intends to maintain the parts of historical decision-making worth replicating, while allowing humans to intervene where historical biases, new research, or noise may render a specific recommendation too risky to automate.

sections.heading: 2 Materials and Methods
sections.text: We describe how we construct the study cohort, fit and calibrate prediction models, quantify uncertainty, combine certified decisions through the Arbitrator, and audit the resulting rules against clinical literature.

sections.heading: 2.1 Data sources and cohort construction
sections.text: We use OPTN PTR match-run data linked to the Standard Transplant Analysis and Research (STAR) deceased donor and waitlist registries for the pooled years 2016--2019 and 2023--2025 to predict whether a deceased donor kidney will be accepted at original PTR sequence number 100 or earlier 2 2 2 This choice was made at the start of this study to remove COVID-19 effects. The 2025 data extend through June 2025. . The PTR dataset records offers made to compatible candidates and their disposition, including bypass, refusal, provisional acceptance, and acceptance. We remove bypassed and date-specific operational-refusal offer rows and exclude donors whose match runs contain out-of-sequence or expedited-placement codes so that the modeled cohort reflects standard on-sequence allocation to the extent observable in the data. We also exclude dual-kidney allocation and selected multiorgan listing pathways whose allocation processes differ from kidney-alone placement. Detailed refusal codes, missing-value handling, feature construction, and leakage exclusions are reported in the Appendix, § S1 – S2 . Kidneys from the same donor are kept within the same data split. Donors are assigned 70% to training, 15% to validation, and 15% to test, stratified by KDPI decile and the number of early-accepted kidneys per donor. The final analysis contains 100,674 training organs, 21,573 validation organs, and 21,574 test organs; the test set contains 14,127 organs (65.5%) accepted within 100 offers and 7,447 (34.5%) not accepted within that cutoff. Training data determine model hyperparameters and probability calibration, validation data determine the uncertainty intervals, and test outcomes are used only for final evaluation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Prediction models and calibration
sections.text: We evaluate six predictors: a thresholded KDPI rule for organs with KDPI ≤ 85 % \leq 85\% , a calibrated KDPI rule, logistic regression, CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost. Logistic regression uses five clinically relevant predictors: creatinine, age, diabetes history, KDPI, and pediatric status. The CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost models are trained on the full donor feature set including demographics, clinical history, serologies, kidney-specific measurements, biopsy variables, and others. For logistic regression, CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost, isotonic calibration is fitted to donor-grouped out-of-fold training predictions. Calibrated KDPI uses isotonic regression fitted to training outcomes using 1 − KDPI / 100 1-\mathrm{KDPI}/100 as the predictor, with KDPI expressed as a percentage. The raw KDPI baseline remains uncalibrated.

sections.heading: 2.3 Local uncertainty
sections.text: Each interpretable model outputs for a specific organ a probability that the organ is EM, a 99% confidence interval for that point prediction, and an interpretable rule that explains why that organ is given that point prediction and confidence level. Here we explain how these confidence intervals are generated for each model. More details can be found in the Appendix, § S3 . For CART, each rule is given by its terminal leaves, so each kidney matches exactly one leaf. We attach the standard Wilson score interval at nominal confidence level 0.99 0.99 [ 44 ] for the fraction of validation organs in each leaf of the trained CART model that are early matchable. In contrast, Random Forest is not naturally an interpretable model, so we turn to Fast Interpretable Rule Extraction (FIRE) [ 23 ] to select a compact set of rules from our trained Random Forest, which we call our SparseRF rule set. We choose to keep at most 128 rules to allow sufficient coverage, which yields 80 selected rules. Each selected rule receives a nominal 99% Wilson interval from matching validation organs. For an organ satisfying multiple validation-supported rules, we take the convex hull of the Wilson intervals for each applicable rule (i.e., we take the lowest lower bound and the highest upper bound out of all of the applicable rules). Consequently, SparseRF certifies an action only when all applicable supported rules certify that same action; otherwise it abstains. If no rule covers an organ, we apply confidence interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] .

The primary operating point for this paper is β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 . In our setting, we do not know the true value p p . Instead, we have its upper and lower bounds with 99% confidence on the validation set given by the Wilson score interval [ L , U ] [L,U] . Equivalently, a model certifies an action only when that action remains optimal across the entire uncertainty interval. The Arbitrator is tasked with resolving the certifications of each of the interpretable models—in our case CART and SparseRF. If both models certify the same action, the Arbitrator uses that action. If exactly one model certifies and the other abstains, the certified action is used. If both abstain or certify conflicting actions, the Arbitrator defers the kidney for organ-level review, represented here by the preference-weighted XGBoost plug-in decision, which uses τ β \tau_{\beta} as the decision threshold.

sections.heading: 2.5 LLM-assisted clinical rule audit
sections.text: We conducted an exploratory literature-assisted audit of the 113 certified contributing rules (35 condensed CART rules 3 3 3 We collapse subtrees whose leaves certify the same action for the sake of conciseness in our analysis. out of 63 originally certified leaves and 78 SparseRF rules) at β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 . We asked a GPT-6-based OpenAI Codex agent to identify 10–20 papers to inform decide/defer/deviate assessments of certified rules, explicitly prioritizing creatinine-driven OOS recommendations for AKI-related reconsideration. The agent selected 18 research papers and one OPTN monitoring report and one clinical guidance document for comparison to the learned rules. The author instructions, agent-selected literature, agent-developed assignment criteria, and limitations are described in the Appendix, § S5.1 .

sections.heading: 3 Results
sections.text: We first compare CART, Random Forest and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) with logistic regression and raw and calibrated KDPI 4 4 4 The Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) is a score from 0% to 100% estimating the percentage of recovered kidneys with lower transplant risk than this kidney. Lower scores proxy higher-functioning kidneys. benchmarks, using donor-only predictors. We evaluate all models on a held-out test set of 21,574 kidneys from the pooled 2016–2019 and 2023–2025 cohort. Of these, 65.5% were early-matchable (EM). Because our goal is to identify transplantable kidneys at risk of discard rather than just identifying poor quality kidneys for OOS allocation, we will often report results on a “low-KDPI” subset of test organs, which we define as kidneys with KDPI below 85 % 85\% 5 5 5 This 85% threshold is meaningful because OPTN policy requires candidates to provide prior written informed consent to receive offers of kidneys with KDPI above 85% [ 34 ] . . This organ subset serves as a proxy for the pool of organs that could potentially be saved if OOS allocation is used. We first show the benefit of ML over clinical heuristics for identifying non-EM organs. We then show that two interpretable models resolve most routing decisions with explicit rules, and we quantify the trade-off between interpretability, average decision cost, and burden on human decision-makers. These high-performing, interpretable base models are inputs into the Arbitrator decision rule, which resolves whether a particular organ has sufficient evidence to be a candidate for automation either OS or OOS. Finally, we illustrate how the resulting rules can be compared to clinical evidence using an agentic AI auditor to ensure that recommended actions align with clinical practice.

sections.heading: 3.1 Comparative Performance of ML Models
sections.text: Figure 2 : ML models identify more non-EM kidneys while recommending fewer EM kidneys for OOS allocation. Each point corresponds to one value of β \beta and shows low-KDPI non-EM kidneys identified for potential OOS placement (y-axis) against low-KDPI EM kidneys unnecessarily routed OOS (x-axis). Stars mark β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 . We assign a cost of 1 to keeping a non-EM organ on-sequence, risking discard (a false positive) and a cost of β \beta to unnecessarily moving an EM organ OOS, unfairly bypassing priority order (a false negative). A model’s average decision cost is the mean of these accumulated costs over all test organs. For each calibrated predictor, the preference parameter β \beta induces a trade-off between keeping EM organs on-sequence and identifying non-EM organs for OOS allocation. Figure 2 traces the resulting trade-off on low-KDPI test kidneys as β \beta varies. Curves further up and to the left are better: they identify more low-KDPI non-EM organs while recommending fewer EM organs for OOS allocation. The ML models improve on the calibrated KDPI baseline, and the trade-off generally improves with model complexity: XGBoost generally outperforms Random Forest, which outperforms CART, which outperforms logistic regression. The Arbitrator, which is discussed further in the next section, is shown for completeness in Figure 2 , but we observe that the Arbitrator approximates Random Forest performance very closely. We use the starred operating point at β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 (which implies a decision threshold of τ 0.5 = 2 / 3 \tau_{0.5}=2/3 ) for the remaining analyses, which weights the benefit of saving an organ from discard at twice the benefit of maintaining the match run. At β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 , XGBoost identifies 66.7% of low-KDPI, non-EM kidneys (3,300 of the total 4,944) for potential OOS placement while unnecessarily routing only 13.7% of low-KDPI, EM kidneys (1,870 of 13,612) out-of-sequence. In contrast, the calibrated KDPI baseline correctly identifies 485 fewer low-KDPI non-EM kidneys for OOS placement than XGBoost while unnecessarily routing 1,111 more EM kidneys OOS, suggesting that a single clinical heuristic is too coarse for the inherent complexity of the prediction. Standard predictive metrics show the same ordering (Appendix, Table S4 ): XGBoost has the highest accuracy and F1 scores and the lowest log loss and average decision cost per organ, followed by Random Forest, CART, logistic regression, and the KDPI baselines. Importantly, CART and Random Forest, the two models on which our interpretable approach builds, recover much of XGBoost’s improvement over the calibrated clinical baseline. At β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 , their accuracies, 0.788 and 0.801, are within 0.027 and 0.014, respectively, of XGBoost’s accuracy of 0.815, compared with the 0.076 gap when comparing XGBoost with calibrated KDPI. Thus, CART and Random Forest clearly outperform the clinical baseline while not deviating too far from black-box XGBoost’s performance. However, none of these models’ point predictions convey whether the evidence behind each prediction is strong enough to act on. We next build an interpretable Arbitrator model to restrict automation to cases with sufficient certainty.

sections.heading: 3.2 Interpretable Resolution with the Arbitrator
sections.text: We use two interpretable models: CART, a single decision tree, and SparseRF, a sparsification of the trained Random Forest that retains a small set of its rules approximating the full Random Forest model. The Arbitrator considers the optimal action prescribed by each model and the relative certainty that the prescribed action would still be optimal on out-of-sample data with high probability. A model certifies an action only when that action remains cost-minimizing throughout its interval; otherwise, it abstains from making a decision. We say an organ receives dual certification if both models certify the same action and single certification if only one of the two interpretable models certifies an action while the other abstains. Our Arbitrator resolves an organ’s routing decision so long as it is single- or dual-certified, and defers all other organs for individual review (see Figure 1 ). In this study, individual review is represented by the XGBoost decision. Certification decisions by interpretable model on the held-out test set are shown in Figure 3 . Figure 3 : CART and SparseRF provide complementary certification. Test kidney certification level at β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 by CART and SparseRF. In Figure 3 , we see that for β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 , CART and SparseRF provided dual certification of the same action for 17,121 kidneys (79.4% of the test set). Single certification pathways covered another 3,060 (14.2%): 1,689 through CART alone and 1,371 through SparseRF alone. The remaining 1,393 (6.5%) had no agreed certified action. sections.heading: 3.3 Modest Cost of Interpretability
sections.text: It is well-known that interpretability comes at a cost, but we ask where this cost arises and how large the decision cost gap is versus our black box XGBoost. We investigate the relative costs of misclassifications on historical data in Table 2 , recognizing the caveat that low prediction error alone is insufficient for making future, high-quality recommendations. We find in Table 2 that the misclassification rates vary significantly by the Arbitrator’s certification pathway. In particular, resolving decisions with interpretable rules comes at essentially no cost relative to XGBoost on dual certified pathways; most of the relative increase in error and decision cost comes from single-certified pathways, allowing us to separate the regions of higher and lower certainty. Most of the 0.014-point accuracy gap can be attributed to the 0.029-point gap in the Arbitrator’s false positive rate relative to XGBoost, meaning that the Arbitrator incorrectly keeps more non-EM kidneys on-sequence than XGBoost. For dual-certified organs, the Arbitrator nearly matches XGBoost’s average cost of 0.108 with only a 4.8% increase to 0.114; for single-certified organs, the gap in the cost attained widens to 28.0% for CART-only certification, and to 20.0% for SparseRF-only certification. The cost gap is localized to the difficult single-certified cases: although single-certified kidneys make up only 14.2% of the test set, they account for about two-thirds of the Arbitrator’s additional cost. Note that decision-making on organs receiving single-model certification was generally harder for all models. In terms of potential impact, the Arbitrator retroactively recommended 1,920 of 2,738 (70.1%) low-KDPI, historically discarded kidneys for OOS placement compared with 2,079 (75.9%) for XGBoost (Appendix, Table S8 ). That is, if our model were deployed retroactively, anywhere between 1,920 and 2,079 patients on the wait list could have received a high-quality organ but were never given the opportunity. Thus, while we see a trade-off in predictive power between interpretable and non-interpretable models, our model demonstrates a high potential impact for saving historically discarded, low-KDPI organs. We next discuss the 1,393 (6.5%) kidneys that the Arbitrator deferred: 1,043 for which both CART and SparseRF abstained due to uncertainty, and 350 for which they certified opposite actions. On this deferred subset, XGBoost has lower accuracy (0.704 vs. 0.853) and higher average cost (0.202 vs. 0.108) than on dually certified kidneys. On the deferred subset, however, XGBoost has higher accuracy and lower average cost than on either single-certified subset. This pattern suggests that some decisions left unresolved by the interpretable models may include decisions better captured by more complex models like XGBoost, while single-certified kidneys remain distinctly challenging, even for XGBoost. A possible hypothesis is that single-certified organs have higher amounts of inherent or aleatoric uncertainty in their outcomes, for which additional model complexity or more data points can do little to improve predictive performance. On the other hand, the deferred organ subset may have more reducible or epistemic uncertainty that XGBoost is able to reduce through increased model complexity. Regardless of the merit of this hypothesis, deferred and single-certified kidneys identify different types of organs on which prediction is challenging. Figure 4 : Arbitration pathway varies across KDPI. Certification pathways for 21,574 held-out kidneys at β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 , grouped by KDPI. We next examine where these harder cases arise in terms of the perceived quality of the organ. Figure 4 considers how deferral, single certification, and dual certification rates vary with KDPI, a normalized metric of organ quality where lower values are preferred. We observe that single certifications and deferrals are most concentrated for organs with KDPI values between 60% and 85%. Deferral from model disagreement or uncertainty more than doubles from 7.1% to 16.0%, and single certification nearly doubles from 18.4% to 36.5% in the 60–70% range. The dual certification rate remains low (55.8%) in the 70–85% range but shoots back up to 94.9% after the clinically relevant 85% threshold. Thus, we observe that these difficult single-certification or uncertified cases happen at intermediate KDPI values, whereas 93.7% and 94.9% of kidneys with KDPI at most 20% or at least 85%, respectively, are dually certified. This result is intuitive: for organs that are cleanly high- or low-quality, the decision is clear, and the average cost of these decisions is low. The predictions are significantly more difficult at intermediate KDPI values where further deterioration can occur if matching does not take place quickly.

sections.heading: 3.4 Auditing the Arbitrator Pathways
sections.text: We have shown that the Arbitrator uses interpretable rules that can be checked before automation, while maintaining competitive performance compared to the black-box XGBoost model. However, this performance is measured against historical decisions, which should not be treated as ground truth. Instead of burdening clinicians with auditing 21,574 individual organs, we can instead have them audit the 113 rules from single-certification and dual-certification pathways. In this work, we show a proof of concept for this approach using a large language model. Before any decision is automated, its relevant rule must be reviewed and receive one of three outcomes: provisionally retained (decide), referred back to human decision-makers on an organ-by-organ basis (defer), or flagged for the opposite action due to new policy or research (deviate), as shown in Figure 1 . Our exploratory audit assessed these 113 certified contributing rules—35 CART subtrees and 78 SparseRF rules—using literature selected by the agent and assignment criteria developed by the agent. It recommended provisionally retaining 62 actions (decide), referring 43 for physician interpretation (defer), and reconsidering eight opposite actions (deviate). All eight candidates propose on-sequence rather than learned out-of-sequence placement: six concern acute kidney injury (AKI) and two concern a sclerosis threshold. If we assume that the LLM’s audit recommendations are well-founded, up to 86.6% (17,471 of 20,181) of the originally resolved kidneys or 81.0% of all 21,574 test kidneys remain eligible for automation. Furthermore, we find that single-certified rules are flagged more often at the audit stage than dual-certified rules. Under the hypothetical audit procedure, 32.4% of single-certified kidneys (990 of 3,060) were recommended for additional review, compared with only 10.0% of dually certified kidneys (1,720 of 17,121; Appendix, Table S10 ). sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: While black-box ML models can accurately predict historical outcomes in complex datasets, high-stakes decision-making cannot rest on merely replicating historical practice. When these decisions are both time-sensitive and life-critical, automating the “easy” cases frees a limited number of human experts to focus on the truly challenging cases. Our contribution is an Arbitrator policy that certifies an interpretable decision rule for possible automation only when (a) the recommendation is sufficiently stable over its relative uncertainty and (b) the rule is audited against clinical literature and explicitly approved for automation. Deceased-donor kidney allocation is such a high-stakes setting: kidneys deteriorate as the match run proceeds, so OPOs must decide relatively quickly whether to continue on-sequence. Automating routing decisions for deceased-donor organs has the potential to reduce organ discard rates while simultaneously ensuring that the fair, standardized offer sequence is used as much as possible. The Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organs with interpretable rules and is able to flag 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI test kidneys for expedited placement (Appendix, Table S8 ). If this test-set performance generalizes, the Arbitrator would flag 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys for potential expedited placement. Applying that share to the 8,418 deceased-donor kidneys recovered for transplant but not used in 2023 [ 14 ] gives a pool of approximately 3,700 kidneys that could have been targeted for expedited placement and potentially saved.

sections.heading: Future Work
sections.text: It is well-known that interpretability comes at some cost to predictive performance, and this is true in our setup as well. We believe this cost is worth paying: self-auditing pipelines let us inspect the trends an AI model has learned, which matters for the ethical deployment of automated systems. We leave the exploration of generation of organ-specific confidence intervals using more complex models like XGBoost or large language models to future work. While our agentic auditor design is intended to be a proof of concept for how LLMs can parse interpretable rules against clinical literature, we leave development of more powerful pipelines to future work. In the organ allocation context, we use the lack of a candidate’s acceptance by original PTR sequence 100 as a proxy for difficult placement, supported by historical acceptance data (Appendix, § S1.5 and Fig. S2 ). Though this is not a clinical metric, other ML work for predicting kidney acceptance outcomes has truncated the PTR sequence to denoise outcomes [ 5 ] . Further, our model predicts the likelihood of organ placement rather than the likelihood of a successful transplant. Since we consider the OS versus OOS allocation decision rather than the success of candidate/donor matching, we believe that predicting the likelihood of organ acceptance is more relevant than predicting post-transplant outcomes; however, transplantation outcomes data would be useful in both (re)designing the organ matching process and refining the auditor in future work. Finally, our current framework determines whether a kidney should leave the standard sequence, not where it should go. This requires the development of a carefully constructed routing system that can account for donor/patient compatibility, ischemia time, and fairness across centers and patients. We leave this to future work. Our framework decides where models are jointly confident, and defers or deviates where their interpretations disagree or are uncertain. More work is needed on the “human” side of this proposed human–AI integration: how uncertainty, deferral, and deviation interact with domain experts, and whether they build trust in the system. Studies of how clinicians and OPO staff interpret, trust, or override certified rules could inform the pre-review audit and the elicitation of our relative preference between sending a non-EM organ on-sequence versus sending an EM organ out-of-sequence. In organ allocation, it also remains open how to separate correlative rules learned by the models (e.g., donor height below 65 cm) from causal rules that withstand clinical scrutiny (e.g., donor age below two years). Refitting or leave-one-out analyses on subpopulations covered by questionable rules could separate clinically meaningful splits from correlated ones. Language-model-assisted review could scale this auditing by retrieving literature, flagging rules for clinical review, and proposing revisions with their estimated performance cost. We believe that our work opens significant avenues for future work, which could help build auditable and trustworthy AI-driven pipelines, specifically for life-critical domains like healthcare.

sections.heading: S1.1 Data sources and the match run
sections.text: The study combines Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) Potential Transplant Recipient (PTR) match-run records with Standard Transplant Analysis and Research (STAR) deceased-donor and waitlist registry data. PTR records preserve the original ranked offer sequence, offer responses, and recorded refusal reasons, whereas the deceased-donor registry supplies donor characteristics and kidney-specific measurements and dispositions. Donor identifiers link the offer histories to registry-derived kidney and donor features. Transplant programs evaluate candidates and register them on the national waiting list. When a deceased-donor organ becomes available, the matching system combines donor and candidate information to generate a match run : a ranked list of biologically compatible candidates under OPTN allocation policy. Kidney matching considers medical and logistical factors, including blood type, immune compatibility, waiting time, expected post-transplant survival (EPTS) scores, and geography United Network for Organ Sharing [] . The organ procurement organization (OPO) communicates offers to transplant programs, which review donor information and may decline or express provisional interest. A provisional acceptance indicates interest in accepting the organ or obtaining further information; it is not final acceptance. When a candidate is the next in the PTR sequence, the program must officially accept or refuse the offer; if it declines, offering can continue to the next candidate in match-run order Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network [] . Prespecified acceptance criteria and offer filters can bypass offers (i.e., automatically decline them) without a new clinical review of each offer United Network for Organ Sharing [2023] . PTR histories therefore include bypasses, refusals, provisional interest, and final acceptance: an original sequence number represents a ranked position rather than a number of deliberate rejections (i.e., some of the preceding offers may have been automatically bypassed). For model development and evaluation, we pool match-run years 2016--2019 and 2023--2025, with observations through June 30, 2025, excluding COVID-19-disrupted years 2020--2022 6 6 6 During the initial U.S. COVID-19 surge, national registry studies documented fewer kidney waitlist registrations and deceased-donor kidney transplants than expected, with larger reductions in states with higher COVID-19 burden Boyarsky et al. [2020] . Kidney recovery, utilization and discard patterns also changed during 2020 Li et al. [2021] . These findings motivate our design choice to remove the pandemic period from consideration in our study. . These disjoint periods span changes in allocation practice and recording conventions, so we maintain the organ recovery year as a feature in the ML models 7 7 7 Match-run year determines source inclusion. Of the 71,913 eligible donors, 28 have recovery dates in adjacent years: two in 2015 and 26 in 2020, with none in 2022. Their 56 kidneys remain in the pooled cohort. . We separately reconstruct the COVID-19-disrupted 2020–2022 match-run cohort using the same source-linkage, offer-filtering, kidney-eligibility, and outcome rules to show how OOS allocation and acceptance outcomes have shifted over time without adding these kidneys to our analysis.

sections.heading: S1.2 Early-matchable outcome
sections.text: Define early-matchability , denoted EM, by Y i = + 1 Y_{i}=+1 only when an eligible final acceptance (denoted by OFFER_ACCEPT=Y ) occurs at original PTR_SEQUENCE_NUM ≤ 100 \leq 100 for kidney i i . Provisional acceptance (denoted by OFFER_ACCEPT=Z ) does not establish the outcome. A kidney without qualifying early final acceptance has Y i = − 1 Y_{i}=-1 , denoted non-EM. We justify our use of the EM cut-off at PTR_SEQUENCE_NUM ≤ 100 \leq 100 in § S1.5 . PTR acceptance records identify the donor but do not identify whether an offer concerns the left or right kidney. We therefore infer kidney-level EM labels from eligible final OFFER_ACCEPT=Y records at original sequence 100 or earlier and the registry’s kidney-specific transplantation status. For a donor with one recorded kidney, at least one early Y labels that kidney EM. For a donor with two recorded kidneys, no early Y labels neither kidney EM, whereas two or more early Y s label both as EM. We have to infer in the case where there is exactly one early Y . In this case, each kidney recorded as transplanted is labeled EM, and each kidney not recorded as transplanted is labeled non-EM. Thus, if both kidneys were transplanted, both are labeled EM despite only one observed early acceptance; if only one was transplanted, only that kidney is labeled EM. This is an assignment convention, rather than a ground truth. This single- Y assignment applies to 16,387 of the 71,913 donors in the primary union (22.79%).

sections.heading: S1.3 Cohort construction
sections.text: We construct the cohort by linking deceased donor records to their generated match run based on the DONOR_ID . A donor can donate up to two organs, and prediction occurs at the kidney level. Each kidney receives the EM label and organ-assignment convention defined in § S1.2 . To study acceptance under standard match-run ordering, we exclude kidneys from donors with recorded indicators of out-of-sequence (OOS) placement. The study uses codes 861 (operational–OPO), 862 (donor medical urgency), 863 (offer not made due to an expedited-placement attempt), and 887 (not offered–expedited placement), which OPTN identifies as indicators of OOS allocation Health Resources and Services Administration [2026] . A code in either refusal field triggers exclusion of the donor’s kidneys. Figure S1 shows the annual fraction of PTR donors with recorded OOS indicators between 2016 and 2025. The PTR refusal-code system changed on December 2, 2021 OPTN Data Advisory Committee [2022] . We therefore apply the historical operational-refusal code list to offers dated before that change and the revised list to offers dated on or after it. sections.heading: S1.4 Donor-grouped splits
sections.text: We randomly assign donors, rather than individual kidneys, to training, validation, and test sets. Keeping both kidneys from the same donor together prevents their shared clinical characteristics and offer history from appearing on both sides of model development and evaluation. Before splitting, each donor is assigned to a stratum defined by the combination of KDPI decile and the number of EM kidneys from that donor (0, 1, or 2). Stratification preserves approximately similar distributions of donor risk and early acceptance across sets (Table S2 ). The split has two stages. First, 70% of donors are assigned to training and the remaining 30% are held aside. Second, those held-aside donors are divided equally between validation and test, producing approximately 70/15/15% donor allocation overall. Both stages use the same strata. The kidney percentages can differ slightly because donors contribute different numbers of retained kidneys. All models use the same donor assignments. Test data are reserved for final evaluation. sections.heading: S1.5 Operational populations and the 100-offer cutoff
sections.text: We use KDPI < 85 % <85\% as an operational policy proxy for whether an organ should be accepted by someone on the match run if there is no further deterioration. Kidneys meeting this criterion are called low-KDPI . We note that kidneys with KDPI above 85% can be transplanted; however OPTN Policy 5.3.C requires transplant programs to obtain written, informed consent before offering such kidneys to a candidate Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network [] due to increased risk of graft failure. From this low-KDPI subset, we consider two base populations. The first is the set of low-KDPI, non-EM organs in the dataset. We interpret this subset as the set of high-quality, historical donor organs that demonstrated elevated risk of discard by maintaining the standard match run. While they may have eventually been accepted after PTR sequence number 100 and transplanted, we identify these organs as possibly being a “close call” that should be avoided. Second, we consider low-KDPI kidneys with recorded explicit discard, identified by codes 503, 504, or 531 in the registry-derived REASON_CD field. Thus, we can proxy the number of transplantable organs saved by our methodology by the number of these low-KDPI originally-discarded organs that would have been recommended for OOS allocation. The 21,574-kidney test set contains 4,944 low-KDPI non-EM kidneys and 2,738 low-KDPI historically discarded kidneys, the populations used in the main-text intervention summaries. Across all training, validation, and test observations from the pooled 2016–2019 and 2023–2025 match-run years, the 143,821-kidney cohort contains 33,068 low-KDPI non-EM kidneys and 18,302 low-KDPI historically discarded kidneys. We prespecified acceptance by original sequence 100 as the threshold for early matchability. A useful threshold should satisfy two conditions: most kidneys that are eventually accepted should be accepted before it, and kidneys still unplaced after it should face substantially higher risk of discard. Figure S2 examines both conditions using two descriptive curves, separated by KDPI value. Cumulative acceptance at sequence k k is the fraction of eventually accepted kidneys that were accepted by sequence k k . Conditional explicit discard at sequence k k is the fraction of kidneys still unplaced when their donor’s match run reaches sequence k k that were ultimately discarded. Both conditions hold at sequence 100. By that point, 91.76% of eventually accepted kidneys with KDPI < 85 % <85\% had been accepted (90.36% across all KDPI values), so the threshold captures most acceptances. Among kidneys still unplaced by the hundredth candidate on the PTR sequence, the pooled probability of explicit discard was 58.46%, compared with 20.35% at the start of the match run, a 2.87-fold increase. A kidney not placed by sequence 100 is therefore not necessarily unusable or destined for discard, but it does face markedly higher risk. These patterns support the 100-offer threshold as a proxy for EM. Figure S2 : Empirical offer-level acceptance and discard statistics. sections.heading: S2.1 Predictors and missingness
sections.text: We train six models: the raw KDPI cutoff at 85%, calibrated KDPI cutoff, logistic regression, CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost. The first three models make use of a limited feature space for prediction. The two KDPI methods only use KDPI thresholding to make predictions. The raw-cutoff model predicts EM whenever KDPI ≤ 85 % \leq 85\% and non-EM otherwise. The calibrated KDPI model fits isotonic regression to training outcomes using 1 − KDPI / 100 1-\mathrm{KDPI}/100 as the predictor, with KDPI expressed as a percentage. Logistic regression uses the five predictors: serum creatinine levels, age, history of diabetes, KDPI, and an indicator of whether or not the patient is a pediatric candidate. CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost are able to make use of the full preprocessed donor feature set. We curate this feature set from 188 source inputs before categorical expansion. Donor identifiers, final disposition, transplantation, acceptance and downstream offer-count evidence are excluded from prediction; transplantation flags above are used only to construct labels. Continuous tree inputs retain native missing values. Categorical predictors are represented by indicator variables for categories observed in the training data; the same encoding is applied to validation and test data.

sections.heading: S2.2 Training and calibration
sections.text: We use training data for model fitting and calibration, while validation data supports rule uncertainty estimates. We reserve test data for final evaluation. In all of the ML models (i.e., excluding both KDPI benchmarks), the trained model is calibrated using isotonic regression on donor-grouped out-of-fold training predictions. For calibrated KDPI, we fit isotonic regression directly to the fixed scores 1 − KDPI 1-\mathrm{KDPI} and observed EM outcomes in the training set. Unlike the ML models, this score does not require fitting a predictive model, so out-of-fold predictions are unnecessary. Every calibrated model is thresholded at the cost-minimizing value τ β = 1 / ( 1 + β ) \tau_{\beta}=1/(1+\beta) , so no decision threshold is tuned on validation data. Held-out evaluation on the test set reports accuracy, log loss, F1 for each class, and average decision cost incurred from false positives (cost of 1) and false negatives (cost of β \beta ). We see in Figure S3 that isotonic calibration fitted on cross-fitted training predictions transfers to the held-out test set. The kidney-weighted mean absolute gap between predicted and observed rates is 0.005–0.011 across models, and no bin with at least 200 kidneys differs by more than 0.06 (CART and XGBoost) or 0.03 (calibrated KDPI, logistic regression and Random Forest). sections.heading: Appendix S3 Validation-supported uncertainty and SparseRF
sections.text: Each interpretable model m ∈ { CART , SRF } m\in\{\mathrm{CART},\mathrm{SRF}\} in the Arbitrator has a set of rules ℛ m \mathcal{R}_{m} over the donor feature space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Each rule r ∈ ℛ m r\in\mathcal{R}_{m} is a conjunction of split conditions that defines a region of 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , and we write x ∈ r x\in r when a kidney with features x x satisfies it (e.g., donor age > 50 >50 years and KDPI ≤ 60 % \leq 60\% and terminal creatinine > 1.5 >1.5 mg/dL and a history of hypertension). For each rule, we attach a 99% confidence interval [ L r , U r ] [L_{r},U_{r}] for the true early-acceptance (EM) rate p r p_{r} of kidneys satisfying r r , computed from validation-set kidneys. For a kidney x x , model m m combines the intervals of the rules it matches, A m ​ ( x ) = { r ∈ ℛ m : x ∈ r } A_{m}(x)=\{r\in\mathcal{R}_{m}:x\in r\} , into a single interval [ L m ​ ( x ) , U m ​ ( x ) ] [L_{m}(x),U_{m}(x)] . This section describes how those intervals are constructed; § S4 describes how they are used to make routing decisions. The two models share three design choices. First, rules are learned from training outcomes only. Second, each rule’s EM rate and its 99% Wilson interval are estimated from the independent validation set, so the same outcomes are never used both to form a rule and to measure its uncertainty. Third, a kidney not covered by any rule with validation support receives the uninformative interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . The models differ in how rules are formed. CART partitions the feature space into disjoint terminal leaves, so every kidney falls in exactly one leaf (§ S3.1 ). A Random Forest has far too many leaves across its trees to audit individually. We therefore use Fast Interpretable Rule Extraction (FIRE) Liu and Mazumder [2023] to select a sparse subset of the forest’s leaves as rules, and we denote the resulting model SparseRF (§ S3.2 ). Unlike CART leaves, SparseRF rules can overlap, so a kidney may match several rules; we combine their intervals into a single conservative interval, the consensus envelope. Furthermore, due to sparsification, it is also possible for an organ not to belong in any of the sparsified rules generated by FIRE.

sections.heading: S3.2 SparseRF: selecting rules with FIRE
sections.text: Each leaf of the fitted Random Forest is a conjunction of split conditions (e.g., KDPI ≤ 60 % \leq 60\% and terminal creatinine ≥ 1.635 \geq 1.635 mg/dL) and therefore defines a candidate rule, but the forest has far too many leaves to audit. We use Fast Interpretable Rule Extraction (FIRE) Liu and Mazumder [2023] , in its sparsity-only form, to extract a small subset of these leaves: FIRE fits a sparse weighted combination of leaf indicators to the training EM labels, and its penalty trades sparsity (i.e., maintaining fewer rules), against coverage (i.e., more kidneys are matched by at least one selected rule). We cap the selection at 128 rules, a fixed design choice made to give SparseRF sufficient coverage (§ S3.4 compares other caps); with this cap, FIRE selects 80 rules, which form SparseRF’s rule set ℛ SRF = 𝒮 ^ \mathcal{R}_{\rm SRF}=\widehat{\mathcal{S}} . Neither validation nor test outcomes are used in this selection, and the FIRE coefficients determine only which rules are kept: each selected rule’s uncertainty comes from its validation Wilson interval (§ S3.3 ).

sections.heading: S4.2 Decision certification under uncertainty
sections.text: Each interpretable model m m used by the Arbitrator supplies a validation-supported Wilson interval [ L m ​ ( x ) , U m ​ ( x ) ] [L_{m}(x),U_{m}(x)] , constructed as described in § S3 . For a model m m making a prediction on organ with feature vector x x , we certify an on-sequence decision ( a m ​ ( x ) = + 1 a_{m}(x)=+1 ) if L m ​ ( x ) > τ β L_{m}(x)>\tau_{\beta} , off-sequence ( a m ​ ( x ) = − 1 a_{m}(x)=-1 ) if U m ​ ( x ) < τ β U_{m}(x)<\tau_{\beta} , and abstain ( a m ​ ( x ) = 0 a_{m}(x)=0 ) otherwise. Certification is therefore a model-level assessment of whether the same action is optimal throughout the entire uncertainty interval. In our two-model Arbitrator framework there are four possible certification pathways across CART and SparseRF: dual (both models certify the same action), CART-only (CART certifies and SparseRF abstains), SparseRF-only (SparseRF certifies and CART abstains), or deferred (both abstain, or they certify opposite actions). The Arbitrator reconciles the possibly different model certifications to decide whether the organ should be routing off-sequence, kept on-sequence, or deferred for expert feedback in a process called resolution . The main text uses the single certification resolution policy, which resolves dually certified kidneys and both single-model pathways. Here we also consider a stricter dual certification policy, which resolves only dually certified kidneys, to show what single-model resolution adds in terms of coverage. Under either policy, all non-resolved kidneys are deferred to organ-level review. Because that review is not observed, our retrospective evaluation assigns each deferred kidney the calibrated XGBoost decision at τ β \tau_{\beta} as a stand-in for an expert reviewer, so every kidney receives a decision, but only resolved kidneys receive an interpretable one. Deferral at this stage reflects statistical uncertainty or disagreement; a separate, later rule-level deferral can arise when an audited rule is not recommended for automation based on clinical research or policy (§ S5 ). The 3,060 total organs that are certified only by CART or SparseRF account for the gap between the two policies’ resolution totals (20,181 versus 17,121), and their downstream average cost. Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation Madeleine Pollack Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139 Thomas Daillak Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139 Mehmet Toner Affiliation: Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02114 Affiliation: Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115 Korkut Uygun Affiliation: Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02114 Affiliation: Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115 Heidi Yeh Affiliation: Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02114 Affiliation: Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115 Swati Gupta Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139 Abstract We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions , defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done rather than what should have been done, and where data is sparse, a model’s predictions may be too uncertain to act on. In this work, we provide a framework for addressing this problem using a case study in deceased-donor kidney allocation. Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. One can use AI to flag kidneys at risk of delayed or failed placement for out-of-sequence (OOS) allocation, but this comes at the cost of bypassing candidates higher on the waitlist. Thus, OOS allocation should only be used when the organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence. Using Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network match-run data from 2016–2019 and 2023–2025 (excluding COVID-19-disrupted years), we build the Arbitrator framework, which combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. Our Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data, and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. We show that the Arbitrator correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as OOS candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement and potentially transplanted. We then exploit the interpretability of the Arbitrator to create an agentic audit comparing the learned rules to published clinical literature in order to flag decision-making patterns that are contentious. We discuss various future directions that stem from this advancement due to AI. Keywords: organ transplantation; machine learning; uncertainty quantification; human–AI decision making; resource allocation 1 Introduction In 2023, nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States were not transplanted despite a persistent and overwhelming shortage of organs for patients with kidney failure [ 21 ] . The problem is not simply that all non-transplanted kidneys are medically unsuitable; rather, many of these organs are likely transplantable upon recovery [ 2 ] , but deteriorate over the length of time required for an organ procurement organization (OPO) to find a suitable match for the organ [ 7 ; 45 ; 3 ] . Under OPTN policy, a deceased donor kidney in the United States is offered sequentially to compatible candidates in a priority sequence, or match run , determined by national allocation rules [ 11 ] . This sequence is designed to make the organ offer process systematic, fair, and auditable. However, if OPOs believe that sequential offering is unlikely to succeed by the time the organ expires, they may choose to expedite placement via out-of-sequence (OOS) placement [ 17 ; 12 ] . This creates a tradeoff: adhering to the match run risks nonuse of hard-to-place organs, while OOS placement bypasses candidates with higher priority, undermining the fairness the match run is designed to ensure. The concern that OOS allocation processes may be unfair is not unmerited: recent work has documented socioeconomic differences among recipients of OOS kidneys [ 17 ; 18 ; 29 ] , and more work is needed to ensure OOS allocation is not exacerbating inequities in the healthcare system. A useful decision aid must therefore distinguish organs for which OOS allocation prevents nonuse from those easily matchable organs for which the standard sequence should be preserved. Machine learning (ML) and, more broadly, artificial intelligence (AI) are attractive tools for this problem because donor profiles are high dimensional and organ acceptance reflects nonlinear interactions between clinical characteristics. Predictive models have already been developed for kidney discard, delayed placement, and offer acceptance [ 27 ; 48 ; 4 ; 5 ; 43 ] . But the barrier to responsible deployment is not predictive performance alone. In a qualitative study of 23 healthcare professionals considering AI-driven clinical decision support for resource allocation, Yüksel Elgin and Elgin found recurring concerns about the cost of increased efficiency in terms of equity, transparency and explainability. Participants also stressed the need for additional review and manual oversight of AI decisions and emphasized that AI should be used for decision support rather than a replacement for clinical expertise [ 47 ] . It is evident that in high-stakes decisions, a model with high predictive accuracy on past data does not imply that the model’s learned behaviors are always worth replicating. AI models trained on historical outcomes can learn and reproduce the bias of the dataset when used for future high-stakes decisions [ 31 ] , and historical organ allocation decisions themselves show socioeconomic disparities [ 17 ; 29 ] . Beyond bias, decision guidelines can also become outdated with new research and evolving transplantation policy, meaning that a good decision using the best available information ten years ago may differ from a good decision using the best available information today. These concerns motivate a shift from prioritizing accuracy in prediction to generating uncertainty-aware prescription. That is, AI models must support decisions about not just how to intervene, but also whether to intervene based on the model’s limitations. Our work seeks to incorporate three relevant components when using AI to recommend kidneys for out-of-sequence allocation: interpretability, uncertainty-awareness, and validation from external evidence. These components are integrated sequentially in our framework in Figure 1 . Figure 1 : Our uncertainty-aware, auditable Arbitrator model. Each interpretable model certifies an action only when its confidence interval lies entirely on one side of τ β \tau_{\beta} . Organs with certified, non-conflicting actions are resolved; all others are deferred. An auditor (expert or language model) checks each resolved rule against clinical references and recommends deciding, deviating, or further deferring. XGBoost handles deferred organs. First, we use interpretable 1 1 1 We define an interpretable model as one whose predictions are defined by a decision rule , e.g., “if KDPI ≤ x \leq x and creatinine ≤ y \leq y and patient age is between z 1 z_{1} and z 2 z_{2} , then predict class C C with probability p p .” ML models to predict the probability that a deceased-donor kidney will be accepted by a patient on the match run within 100 offers. We call this outcome early-matchability (EM), and we recommend that OOS allocation be considered when an organ is not likely to be EM. Given a relative preference β \beta for maintaining the match run versus routing high-risk organs OOS, the optimal action is to send an organ OOS if its EM probability is at most τ β \tau_{\beta} . However, a given ML/AI prediction is not guaranteed to be accurate, and different predictions can come with different levels of certainty based on the organ’s features. Our models are uncertainty-aware , which means that the model abstains from making a decision if its confidence interval for the EM probability contains τ β \tau_{\beta} ; that is, if the uncertainty in the estimated EM probability could change the recommended action. Otherwise, the model certifies either the on-sequence (OS) action (the full confidence interval lies above τ β \tau_{\beta} ) or the OOS action (the full confidence interval lies below τ β \tau_{\beta} ). Because we have multiple interpretable ML models, we use the Arbitrator decision rule to resolve their recommendations, submitting either a certified action or deferring the organs for additional review, which, in practice, can be done by humans. In this work, we defer the decision to a more powerful, but “black-box” XGBoost model. Finally, because each model outputs a set of interpretable decision rules, we audit each resolved recommendation for alignment with published medical literature instead of blindly replicating historical decisions. This helps us identify problematic trends learned by AI models from historic data. Our agentic auditor can make one of three decisions: (1) provisionally retain the proposed optimal action (decide), (2) propose considering the opposite action due to medical research (deviate), or (3) request additional review for the model rule and recommendation due to insufficient evidence (defer). This model intends to maintain the parts of historical decision-making worth replicating, while allowing humans to intervene where historical biases, new research, or noise may render a specific recommendation too risky to automate. 2 Materials and Methods We describe how we construct the study cohort, fit and calibrate prediction models, quantify uncertainty, combine certified decisions through the Arbitrator, and audit the resulting rules against clinical literature. 2.1 Data sources and cohort construction We use OPTN PTR match-run data linked to the Standard Transplant Analysis and Research (STAR) deceased donor and waitlist registries for the pooled years 2016--2019 and 2023--2025 to predict whether a deceased donor kidney will be accepted at original PTR sequence number 100 or earlier 2 2 2 This choice was made at the start of this study to remove COVID-19 effects. The 2025 data extend through June 2025. . The PTR dataset records offers made to compatible candidates and their disposition, including bypass, refusal, provisional acceptance, and acceptance. We remove bypassed and date-specific operational-refusal offer rows and exclude donors whose match runs contain out-of-sequence or expedited-placement codes so that the modeled cohort reflects standard on-sequence allocation to the extent observable in the data. We also exclude dual-kidney allocation and selected multiorgan listing pathways whose allocation processes differ from kidney-alone placement. Detailed refusal codes, missing-value handling, feature construction, and leakage exclusions are reported in the Appendix, § S1 – S2 . Kidneys from the same donor are kept within the same data split. Donors are assigned 70% to training, 15% to validation, and 15% to test, stratified by KDPI decile and the number of early-accepted kidneys per donor. The final analysis contains 100,674 training organs, 21,573 validation organs, and 21,574 test organs; the test set contains 14,127 organs (65.5%) accepted within 100 offers and 7,447 (34.5%) not accepted within that cutoff. Training data determine model hyperparameters and probability calibration, validation data determine the uncertainty intervals, and test outcomes are used only for final evaluation. 2.2 Prediction models and calibration We evaluate six predictors: a thresholded KDPI rule for organs with KDPI ≤ 85 % \leq 85\% , a calibrated KDPI rule, logistic regression, CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost. Logistic regression uses five clinically relevant predictors: creatinine, age, diabetes history, KDPI, and pediatric status. The CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost models are trained on the full donor feature set including demographics, clinical history, serologies, kidney-specific measurements, biopsy variables, and others. For logistic regression, CART, Random Forest, and XGBoost, isotonic calibration is fitted to donor-grouped out-of-fold training predictions. Calibrated KDPI uses isotonic regression fitted to training outcomes using 1 − KDPI / 100 1-\mathrm{KDPI}/100 as the predictor, with KDPI expressed as a percentage. The raw KDPI baseline remains uncalibrated. 2.3 Local uncertainty Each interpretable model outputs for a specific organ a probability that the organ is EM, a 99% confidence interval for that point prediction, and an interpretable rule that explains why that organ is given that point prediction and confidence level. Here we explain how these confidence intervals are generated for each model. More details can be found in the Appendix, § S3 . For CART, each rule is given by its terminal leaves, so each kidney matches exactly one leaf. We attach the standard Wilson score interval at nominal confidence level 0.99 0.99 [ 44 ] for the fraction of validation organs in each leaf of the trained CART model that are early matchable. In contrast, Random Forest is not naturally an interpretable model, so we turn to Fast Interpretable Rule Extraction (FIRE) [ 23 ] to select a compact set of rules from our trained Random Forest, which we call our SparseRF rule set. We choose to keep at most 128 rules to allow sufficient coverage, which yields 80 selected rules. Each selected rule receives a nominal 99% Wilson interval from matching validation organs. For an organ satisfying multiple validation-supported rules, we take the convex hull of the Wilson intervals for each applicable rule (i.e., we take the lowest lower bound and the highest upper bound out of all of the applicable rules). Consequently, SparseRF certifies an action only when all applicable supported rules certify that same action; otherwise it abstains. However, this performance is measured against historical decisions, which should not be treated as ground truth. Instead of burdening clinicians with auditing 21,574 individual organs, we can instead have them audit the 113 rules from single-certification and dual-certification pathways. In this work, we show a proof of concept for this approach using a large language model. Before any decision is automated, its relevant rule must be reviewed and receive one of three outcomes: provisionally retained (decide), referred back to human decision-makers on an organ-by-organ basis (defer), or flagged for the opposite action due to new policy or research (deviate), as shown in Figure 1 . Our exploratory audit assessed these 113 certified contributing rules—35 CART subtrees and 78 SparseRF rules—using literature selected by the agent and assignment criteria developed by the agent. It recommended provisionally retaining 62 actions (decide), referring 43 for physician interpretation (defer), and reconsidering eight opposite actions (deviate). All eight candidates propose on-sequence rather than learned out-of-sequence placement: six concern acute kidney injury (AKI) and two concern a sclerosis threshold. If we assume that the LLM’s audit recommendations are well-founded, up to 86.6% (17,471 of 20,181) of the originally resolved kidneys or 81.0% of all 21,574 test kidneys remain eligible for automation. Furthermore, we find that single-certified rules are flagged more often at the audit stage than dual-certified rules. Under the hypothetical audit procedure, 32.4% of single-certified kidneys (990 of 3,060) were recommended for additional review, compared with only 10.0% of dually certified kidneys (1,720 of 17,121; Appendix, Table S10 ). When these decisions are both time-sensitive and life-critical, automating the “easy” cases frees a limited number of human experts to focus on the truly challenging cases. Our contribution is an Arbitrator policy that certifies an interpretable decision rule for possible automation only when (a) the recommendation is sufficiently stable over its relative uncertainty and (b) the rule is audited against clinical literature and explicitly approved for automation. Deceased-donor kidney allocation is such a high-stakes setting: kidneys deteriorate as the match run proceeds, so OPOs must decide relatively quickly whether to continue on-sequence. Automating routing decisions for deceased-donor organs has the potential to reduce organ discard rates while simultaneously ensuring that the fair, standardized offer sequence is used as much as possible. The Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organs with interpretable rules and is able to flag 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI test kidneys for expedited placement (Appendix, Table S8 ). If this test-set performance generalizes, the Arbitrator would flag 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys for potential expedited placement. Applying that share to the 8,418 deceased-donor kidneys recovered for transplant but not used in 2023 [ 14 ] gives a pool of approximately 3,700 kidneys that could have been targeted for expedited placement and potentially saved. Future Work It is well-known that interpretability comes at some cost to predictive performance, and this is true in our setup as well. We believe this cost is worth paying: self-auditing pipelines let us inspect the trends an AI model has learned, which matters for the ethical deployment of automated systems. We leave the exploration of generation of organ-specific confidence intervals using more complex models like XGBoost or large language models to future work. While our agentic auditor design is intended to be a proof of concept for how LLMs can parse interpretable rules against clinical literature, we leave development of more powerful pipelines to future work. In the organ allocation context, we use the lack of a candidate’s acceptance by original PTR sequence 100 as a proxy for difficult placement, supported by historical acceptance data (Appendix, § S1.5 and Fig. S2 ). Though this is not a clinical metric, other ML work for predicting kidney acceptance outcomes has truncated the PTR sequence to denoise outcomes [ 5 ] . Further, our model predicts the likelihood of organ placement rather than the likelihood of a successful transplant. Since we consider the OS versus OOS allocation decision rather than the success of candidate/donor matching, we believe that predicting the likelihood of organ acceptance is more relevant than predicting post-transplant outcomes; however, transplantation outcomes data would be useful in both (re)designing the organ matching process and refining the auditor in future work. Finally, our current framework determines whether a kidney should leave the standard sequence, not where it should go. This requires the development of a carefully constructed routing system that can account for donor/patient compatibility, ischemia time, and fairness across centers and patients.
